'''''Costus comosus''''', known as '''red tower ginger''', is a [[species]] of plant native to South Mexico to Ecuador.<ref name="NTBG">{{cite web |title=Costus comosus |url=https://ntbg.org/database/plants/detail/costus-comosus |website=Tropical Plant Database - Plant Details |publisher=National Tropical Botanical Garden |access-date=26 July 2024}}</ref><ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=Costus comosus (Jacq.) Roscoe|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:796280-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanical Gardens Kew |access-date=25 July 2024}}</ref>

As a cultivated plant,''Costus comosus'' is cold hardy; however, if it freezes back to the ground over the winter it is unlikely to flower.<ref name="Skinner2016">{{cite journal |last1=Skinner |first1=Dave |title=Ornamental Costus |journal=  Ornamental Horticulture|date=2016 |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=307–317 |url=https://www.academia.edu/download/69904025/672.pdf |doi=10.14295/OH.V22I3.984}}</ref> 

''Costus comosus'' contains chemical compounds which have been found to have anti-diabetic activity.<ref name="Plants">{{cite journal |last1=Bhattacharya |first1=S. |last2=Gupta |first2=N. |last3=Flekalová |first3=A. |last4=Gordillo-Alarcón |first4=S. |last5=Espinel-Jara |first5=V. |last6=Fernández-Cusimamani |first6=E. |title=Exploring Folklore Ecuadorian Medicinal Plants and Their Bioactive Components Focusing on Antidiabetic Potential: An Overview |journal=Plants |date=2024 |volume=13 |issue=1436 |page=1436 |doi=10.3390/plants13111436|doi-access=free |pmid=38891245 |pmc=11174784 }}</ref> In traditional medicine, ''Costus comosus'' is used to treat several conditions including asthma, bronchitis, intestinal worms, diabetes, and liver diseases. It is also used traditionally for rash and fever. People of Southern Ecuador use ''Costus comosus'' to treat headache, liver pain, diabetes, influenza, and kidney ailments.<ref name="JEthnoPharm">{{cite journal |last1=Tene |first1=Vicente |last2=Malagón |first2=Omar |last3=Finzi |first3=Paola Vita |last4=Vidari |first4=Giovanni |last5=Armijos |first5=Chabaco |last6=Zaragoza |first6=Tomás |title=An ethnobotanical survey of medicinal plants used in Loja and Zamora-Chinchipe, Ecuador |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |date=2007 |volume=111 |issue=1 |pages=63–81 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2006.10.032 |pmid=17137737|url=http://dspace.utpl.edu.ec/handle/123456789/19314 }}</ref> They also use it as a diuretic.

The name ''[[Costus barbatus]]'' has often been mistakenly applied to ''Costus comosus''.<ref name="Skinner">{{cite journal |last1=Skinner |first1=Dave |title=Will the REAL Costus barbatus PLEASE STAND UP! |journal=Heliconia Society International Bulletin |date=December 2011 |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=11–14 |url=https://media.wix.com/ugd/ef1aa2_949407aaa98e4fa7a30ba1715f1bc0b5.pdf}}</ref>
